title: scXpand: Pan-cancer detection of T cell clonal expansion from single-cell RNA sequencing without paired single-cell TCR sequencing.
data_url: Trained models only: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30067666 (CC BY 4.0, 1,393,056,068 bytes). Code: https://github.com/yizhak-lab-ccg/scXpand (MIT). The labelled dataset itself is not deposited; Table S1 lists 34 GEO series plus ArrayExpress E-MTAB-10607, Zenodo record 10672442, an SRA SRZ190804 link, a UCL DOI and lambrechtslab.sites.vib.be (EGAS00001004809).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC search on the DOI returned exactly 1 hit (PMID 42567166, PMC13576724, open access, licence 'cc by', Cell Genomics volume 6 issue 9, first published 2026-08-07). I downloaded the full text XML (268,521 bytes) and read the abstract, Results, 'Limitations of the study', 'Data and code availability' and every STAR Methods subsection. FIGSHARE (models): the record 10.6084/m9.figshare.30067666.v1 'scXpand - Trained Models' is public, CC BY 4.0, 1,393,056,068 bytes total; I listed all 27 files via the Figshare application programming interface and downloaded the three small ones myself. gene_table_for_scXpand.csv.gz (91,305 bytes) decompresses to exactly 11,950 data rows with columns gene_ids / gene_name / feature_types, 11,950 unique Ensembl gene identifiers, 11,950 unique gene symbols, and 'Gene Expression' as the only feature type. data_format.json (287,000 bytes) states n_genes = 11950, target_sum = 10000.0, use_log_transform = false, use_zscore_norm = true, aux_categorical_types = empty, and its gene list is byte-identical and in identical order to the gene table. parameters.json (1,004 bytes) holds the logistic-regression hyperparameters. The two deep-learning checkpoints are 597,073,611 and 791,029,067 bytes, over my 50 MB download rule, so I recorded their sizes from the application programming interface rather than downloading; the three shallow models are 49,037, 144,959 and 2,876,308 bytes. GITHUB: repository yizhak-lab-ccg/scXpand, MIT licence, 20,646 KB, created 2025-09-09, last push 2026-08-11, 19 stars; I read README.md (9,899 bytes), docs/data_format.rst (3,984 bytes) and both tutorial notebooks. docs/data_format.rst is decisive: the framework requires the USER to supply an .h5ad file whose cell table already contains 'expansion' ("expanded"/"non-expanded"), 'clone_id_size', 'median_clone_size', 'study', 'patient', 'sample', 'cancer_type', 'tissue_type' and 'imputed_labels', all marked 'Training only'. SUPPLEMENTARY TABLES: Europe PMC's bundle endpoint never completed (40,633,203 bytes in 540 seconds, then 39,604,457 bytes in a second 1,700-second attempt) and PMC's per-file links return HTTP 404, so I located the local file headers inside the two partial streams and raw-inflated the three spreadsheets myself: mmc2.xlsx = Table S1 (31,613 bytes), mmc3.xlsx = Table S2 (401,437 bytes), mmc4.xlsx = Table S3 (54,049 bytes). All three opened as valid Excel files and I parsed every sheet with my own pure-Python reader. From Table S1 I summed the columns myself: tumour training 24 dataset rows, 623 samples, 1,055,922 cells; blood training 11 rows, 340 samples, 532,387 cells; test 12 rows, 482 samples, 1,022,391 cells; 'additional datasets' 3 rows, 57 samples, 350,819 cells. Training total 1,588,309 cells across 963 samples; training plus test = 2,610,700, which is the abstract's '2.6 million'. From Table S2 sheet '2. Model Metrics' I read the five published validation numbers: autoencoder area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve 0.92384, area under the precision-recall curve 0.78264, Matthews correlation coefficient 0.65669, precision 0.6551, recall 0.8760; the five models span 0.91621 to 0.92634 and 0.74241 to 0.78522, matching the paper's stated '0.916-0.926' and '0.742-0.785'. Table S2 sheet '3. Stratified Metrics' is the important one: inside tumour CD8-positive T cells the autoencoder scores only 0.7771, against 0.9116 in blood CD8-positive cells, and tumour CD4-positive precision-recall area is 0.4036. Table S3 sheet '1. Test Datasets - ROC AUC' gives all 12 external datasets for all five models (autoencoder 0.84716 on Zheng oesophageal tumour up to 0.96300 on Shu liver blood, matching the paper's '0.847-0.963') plus a 'Missing Genes per Dataset' column running 0 to 1,086; Table S3 sheet '3. Stratified Metrics' repeats the collapse (tumour CD8-positive 0.7624, blood CD8-positive 0.9133, blood regulatory-T-cell precision-recall area 0.0539). Table S3 sheet '4. SHAP Gene Ranking' has 5,017 rows with NKG7 top. SOURCE DATA: 34 unique GEO accessions appear in the article XML. I listed the GEO file servers directly: GSE169246_TNBC_RNA.counts.mtx.gz is 2,006,028,402 bytes (HTTP Content-Length, not downloaded); GSE179994 holds a 46,213,120-byte RAW.tar plus per-sample Seurat .rds.gz files of about 46 MB each; GSE176021 holds a RAW.tar plus two .rds.gz annotation files. Zenodo record 10672442 (Wang et al. 2024 glioblastoma, the authors' own training-data tutorial example) is open with 6 files totalling 50,851,979,501 bytes, of which Raw_files.zip is 666,868,659 bytes (HTTP Content-Length, not downloaded) and the Zenodo licence field is null. I fetched lambrechtslab.sites.vib.be and confirmed the Bassez et al. 2021 cohorts (Table S1 tumour rows 11 and 12, 80 samples, 36,701 cells) sit behind EGAS00001004809 / EGAD00001006608 with a UZLeuven-VIB data access committee review and a Data Transfer Agreement. Finally, the authors' committed notebook docs/notebooks/data_preparation_tutorial.ipynb contains saved outputs from a real run on that Zenodo record: 92,033 cells x 23,328 genes after RNA quality control, T-cell-receptor quality control cascading 51,779 paired-chain cells to 55,534 to 42,834 to 39,079, and a final per-sample expansion table which I summed to 36,875 labelled cells (8,683 expanded, 23.5%; 28,192 non-expanded) across 26 sample groups. Those are the authors' numbers from their own committed run, not my own execution.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: I never downloaded a single count matrix and never ran a model, so every performance number I quote is the authors' own, read out of their spreadsheets rather than reproduced. I could not read mmc1.pdf (Figures S1-S27) or mmc5.pdf: this machine has no PDF renderer and both sat inside the supplementary bundle I could not fully retrieve, so everything that exists only as a figure is paper-claim-only for me. That includes: the SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) interpretation panels; the analysis of 336,363 CD8-positive T cells across 359 tumour samples from five annotated test datasets, with naive/memory area under the curve 0.77; the comparisons against the NeoTCR8 243-gene signature, the MANAscore, the TR30 signature and the Hanada CD8 transcriptome signature (Figures S23-S25), all of which the text says scXpand beat but for which I retrieved no number; the label-permutation negative control that the Methods say gave 'near-random performance'; the training-set subsampling curve; the patient-level versus sample-level relabelling comparison; the expansion-threshold sensitivity analysis; and the Spearman correlation of 0.319-0.341 between predicted probability and clone size. Also paper-text-only: the training hardware (a 256 GB-memory workstation with a 48 GB graphics card), the claim that 11,950 genes were shared across all datasets (I verified the gene table has 11,950 rows but not that this is the intersection), the claim of 99.78% concordance between clonotype definitions, and the assertion that imputed expression was used 'solely for cell type classification'. I did not verify that any of the 34 GEO series actually contains usable paired T-cell-receptor data, only that the series exist and that their file listings are open.

a1_downloadable.note: FAILS, and it is a split verdict worth stating precisely. What IS downloadable and what I opened myself: the MIT-licensed code, the five trained models on Figshare (CC BY 4.0, no login), and all three supplementary spreadsheets. What is NOT downloadable is the thing an ML project needs - the curated 2.6-million-cell table with expansion labels. It is deposited nowhere: the data availability statement says only 'This paper analyzes existing, publicly available scRNA/TCR-seq data' with accessions in Table S1, plus 'Any additional information required to reanalyze the data reported in this paper is available from the lead contact upon request', which is the checklist's literal 'available on request' fail. I searched Figshare for 'scXpand' (one record, models only) and Zenodo (zero hits). Worse, at least one training cohort is genuinely gated: Bassez et al. 2021 (Table S1 tumour rows 11-12, 80 samples, 36,701 cells) resolves to EGAS00001004809 / EGAD00001006608, and the lab's own page, which I fetched, says access 'will have to be reviewed by the UZLeuven-VIB data access committee' under a Data Transfer Agreement. An EGA access application is an explicit A1 fail condition.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS, and this is the cleanest kill. The thing being predicted - whether a T cell belongs to a clonally expanded clone - is a column in no file anywhere. I verified this from the authors' own specification, docs/data_format.rst, which lists 'expansion' as a field the USER must supply. Building it means, per the authors' own 90-cell notebook: match scRNA-seq to scTCR-seq cell barcode by barcode across two modalities, filter multichain and orphan-chain cells, define clonotypes by exact identity of the CDR3 nucleotide sequence in both receptor chains, concatenate patient and an expression-imputed cell-subtype label into a clone identifier, count clone size per sample, take the median clone size per sample excluding singletons, and threshold at 1.5 times that median. That is 'construct the thing you are predicting' in six steps across two data types, repeated 34 times.

a3_inputs_present.note: Passes. The input is a raw unique-molecular-identifier count matrix, which is what the GEO and Zenodo deposits actually contain, and the exact 11,950-gene feature space is published as a 91 KB file I downloaded and counted (11,950 unique Ensembl identifiers, no duplicates, identical and in identical order to the gene list baked into data_format.json). Two frictions, not killers: many source datasets ship gene symbols rather than Ensembl identifiers so a conversion is needed, and the formats are heterogeneous (.mtx.gz, .rds.gz Seurat objects, RAW.tar, 10x filtered_contig_annotations.csv) across 34 deposits.

a4_units_stated.note: Passes cleanly, which is to the authors' credit. Expression is integer unique-molecular-identifier counts, stated explicitly in docs/data_format.rst ('Raw gene expression counts (non-negative integers)', 'Normalized or log-transformed data is not supported'), and the exact normalisation is machine-readable in data_format.json, which I opened: target_sum 10000.0, use_log_transform false, use_zscore_norm true. Clone size is a cell count. No ambiguity anywhere.

a5_enough_rows.note: Passes by a wide margin at every unit of analysis. I summed Table S1 myself: 1,588,309 training cells across 963 samples and 1,022,391 test cells across 482 samples, 2,610,700 in total. Even the single smallest viable route - the one Zenodo brain record - yields 36,875 labelled cells across 26 samples according to the authors' committed notebook output. Sample size is the one thing that is not a problem here.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: Paper scale: hundreds of gigabytes of download across 34 deposits (one single file, GSE169246_TNBC_RNA.counts.mtx.gz, is 2,006,028,402 bytes compressed by HTTP header) and a 1,588,309 x 11,950 matrix that is 75.9 GB dense in 32-bit floats. Narrowest viable route: the 666,868,659-byte Zenodo Raw_files.zip giving about 1.8 GB dense for 36,875 cells.
a6_fits_laptop.note: FAILS at the paper's scale, and the authors effectively confirm it: they trained on a 256 GB-memory workstation with a 48 GB graphics card. Rebuilding the database needs 34 heterogeneous downloads, and the Zenodo record alone totals 50,851,979,501 bytes. The one heavy step even on a single dataset is MAGIC imputation over 92,033 x 23,328 cells (about 8.6 GB dense before the graph diffusion), which is marginal on 16 GB. By CLAUDE.md's size filter this is squarely a deprioritised raw single-cell resource.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Passes, and unusually well - this is the strongest part of the deposit. My own sums of Table S1 reproduce 1,055,922 tumour cells and 532,387 blood cells exactly as stated in the Figure 1 text, 963 training samples, 482 test samples, and 2,610,700 total against the abstract's '2.6 million'. The gene table has exactly 11,950 rows as claimed. Table S2's model metrics fall exactly inside the quoted 0.916-0.926 and 0.742-0.785 ranges, and Table S3's per-dataset values exactly span the quoted 0.847-0.963. One small discrepancy: Table S1 lists the Wang et al. brain test dataset as 25 samples / 37,009 cells, while the authors' own committed notebook run on that same record yields 26 sample groups and 36,875 cells by my sum.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAILS partially, in a way I traced in the code rather than inferring. The good news first: the label's root is a real physical measurement - CDR3 receptor sequences from single-cell T-cell-receptor sequencing - not another model's output. The problem is the intermediate. The clone identifier is built as patient + clonotype + 'imputed_labels', and 'imputed_labels' (CD8-positive / CD4-positive / regulatory / double-positive / double-negative) comes from MAGIC-imputed expression of CD8A, CD8B, CD4 and FOXP3 - i.e. from the model's own input features. So which cells count as one clone, and therefore clone size and the expansion label, depend partly on a function of the features, which is the checklist's 'even partly, even through an intermediate' leakage. The authors' own stratified tables quantify the damage: the headline 0.924 falls to 0.776 (validation) and 0.762 (test) once you look only inside tumour CD8-positive T cells, and CD8A is the third-ranked SHAP gene with CD8B also in the top 20. Two mitigations I should state fairly: the model is fed non-imputed counts, and the Methods report a label-permutation retrain that collapsed to near-random - though permutation destroys the subtype signal too, so it does not test this specific leak. Second, smaller provenance issue: the threshold is relative (1.5 times the per-sample median), so the label also depends on each sample's overall repertoire composition.

existing_models.name: scXpand itself (five models in one framework: a multi-task count autoencoder, a multilayer perceptron, LightGBM gradient boosting, logistic regression and a support vector machine)
existing_models.score_and_split: I read these out of the authors' own spreadsheets. Validation (patients held out entirely, stratified by tissue and cancer type): area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve 0.91621-0.92634 across the five models, precision-recall area 0.74241-0.78522, best Matthews correlation coefficient 0.65669 (autoencoder). Twelve fully external datasets: autoencoder 0.84716-0.96300. The honest number is lower and the authors published it themselves: inside tumour CD8-positive T cells only, 0.7624 on test and 0.7771 on validation, and blood regulatory-T-cell precision-recall area is 0.0539.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Four things, stated in 'Limitations of the study': performance is 'comparatively reduced' in exhausted and terminally exhausted T cells, which they attribute to receptor-sequencing undersampling rather than model error; the framework 'does not address the actual clonal identity of T cells or their TCR sequence identity'; five cancer types are absent (pancreatic, ovarian, gastric, cervical, haematologic) as are lymph-node and adjacent-normal tissue; and extension to spatial transcriptomics awaits that technology maturing.

existing_models.name: NeoTCR8 (a 243-gene expression signature for neoantigen-reactive tumour-infiltrating CD8-positive T cells)
existing_models.score_and_split: The gene list is published by its own authors. The scXpand text says it 'did not manage to properly differentiate between expanded and non-expanded CD8+ T cells' across all three differentiation states, with lower area under the curve than scXpand - but that result lives only in Figure S23A, which I could not open, so I have no number. A separate paper I found in search reports NeoTCR8 at accuracy 0.47 and area under the curve 0.65 on its own benchmark.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I did not open the primary paper.

existing_models.name: MANAscore (a signature-scoring method for mutation-associated neoantigen-specific T cells, Zeng et al.)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported by the scXpand authors as inferior to scXpand at predicting clonal expansion for both virus-specific and non-virus-specific T cells (Figures S24A-S24B). Figure-only, so no number retrieved by me.

existing_models.name: TR30 (Meng et al.) and the CD8 Transcriptome Signature (Hanada et al.), two published tumour-reactivity gene signatures
existing_models.score_and_split: Both reported as lower-performing than scXpand in Figures S23C and S23D, which I could not open. A third-party comparison I found in search puts the Hanada signature at accuracy 0.77 and area under the curve 0.76 on a different benchmark.

existing_models.name: TRTpred and predicTCR (two 2024 Nature Biotechnology machine-learning predictors of tumour-reactive T cells from single-cell RNA sequencing)
existing_models.score_and_split: Adjacent task, not the same one: they predict tumour reactivity, not clonal expansion. TRTpred was built on 235 CD8-positive clonotypes from ten melanoma patients (112 reactive, 123 not). predicTCR is reported to beat NeoTCR8, Hanada and Caushi signatures. Read from search-result summaries and abstracts only; I did not retrieve the primary papers or verify weight availability.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Both are reported to model clone structure, which other single-cell-level methods do not; intra-clonal heterogeneity is named in the surrounding literature as the open part.

existing_models.name: A pan-immunotherapy expansion signature (Nature Communications 2025), a transcriptomic signature in PD-1-positive Ly108-positive precursor-exhausted cells that predicts rates of intratumoral clone expansion
existing_models.score_and_split: This is the closest independent competitor to the actual task: reported to predict intratumoral clone expansion rates in mice with and without immunotherapy and in patients on PD-1 blockade. I read only the search-result summary and quote no number; weight and code availability unverified.

existing_models.name: Shorer et al. 2025, Cell Genomics (the same laboratory's prior single-cell meta-analysis, 767,606 T cells across 460 samples)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a predictor of expansion from expression; it derives a response signature from already-known expanded CD8-positive clones. It is the source of the 1.5-times-median expansion definition reused here. Open access, Cell Genomics, PMC12143341.

backbone.name: scGPT or Geneformer (large transformer models pretrained on tens of millions of single-cell transcriptomes, both with open weights) are the right shape for this data type, and would be the obvious thing to freeze and fit a head to - the authors notably did not try either, using instead a from-scratch count autoencoder and four off-the-shelf classifiers.
backbone.hardware: Not on this laptop at the paper's scale. Caching Geneformer or scGPT embeddings for 1.6 million cells needs a graphics card; on a 37,000-cell single-dataset subset it would be perhaps a few hours of processor time, but that subset is not the paper's task. The authors used a 48 GB graphics card. Running their released shallow models (logistic regression 49 KB, support vector machine 145 KB, LightGBM 2.9 MB) is genuinely processor-only and cheap - but that is inference, not training.
backbone.licence: scGPT and Geneformer weights are openly available; scXpand's code is MIT and its released checkpoints are CC BY 4.0. The blocking licence issue is upstream: the Zenodo record 10672442 has a null licence field, and the Bassez cohort requires a Data Transfer Agreement.

integration.partner_dataset: Table S1 carries treatment-response annotation that nothing in the released models uses: I counted 546 tumour samples and 276 blood samples with responder/non-responder status split by pre- and post-treatment. The natural partners are the same laboratory's Shorer et al. 2025 immunotherapy meta-analysis (767,606 T cells, 460 samples) and VDJdb, the curated T-cell-receptor epitope database the authors already used for annotation.
integration.join_key: Ensembl gene identifiers (11,950 of them, verified by me in the released gene table) for anything gene-level; GEO series accession plus patient identifier for sample-level joins; CDR3 amino-acid sequence for VDJdb. All are standard, present and clean.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does clonal expansion predicted from expression alone in a pre-treatment tumour biopsy predict checkpoint-inhibitor response in the hundreds of cohorts that were never receptor-sequenced? That is a genuinely bigger question than either dataset answers alone, and it is the obvious next paper - but it needs the labelled database, which is exactly what is not deposited.

controls.positive_control: Unusually good if the data existed, and partly already run: the authors report that mean predicted probability per clone correlates with actual clone size (Spearman 0.319-0.341), which any working pipeline must recover. A second, cheaper one: CD8A and NKG7 must come out as top positive drivers and SELL, CCR7 and LEF1 as top negative drivers, because the authors published that exact ranking in Table S3 sheet 4 (5,017 rows, which I parsed) - so the SHAP ordering is a published answer key.
controls.negative_control: Also already run by the authors, which removes most of the project's value: they retrained all five models from scratch on permuted expansion labels and report near-random performance. The one negative control they did NOT run, and the one that matters for the leak I found, is to shuffle only the imputed-subtype term inside the clone identifier and re-derive the labels, which would isolate how much of the headline 0.924 is the model re-deriving the cell-type label that went into its own ground truth.
controls.external_validation: Exemplary and already published: 12 fully external datasets, 482 samples, 1,022,391 cells, with per-dataset and per-model numbers in Table S3 which I parsed myself, plus two liver-cancer cohorts of a cancer type absent from training, plus adjacent-normal tissue, plus a non-cancer colon-biopsy cohort. There is nothing left to add here.

honest_claim_h3: The most anyone could honestly claim from a reproduction here is: 'from raw single-cell gene-expression counts, this ranks whether a tumour-infiltrating or blood T cell belongs to a clone whose size exceeds 1.5 times the median clone size in its own sample, as measured by single-cell receptor sequencing in 14 cancer types, with area under the curve around 0.92 when blood and tumour and all T-cell subtypes are pooled but only around 0.76 inside tumour CD8-positive T cells where the question actually matters' - and the authors have already published both of those numbers themselves.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a T cell's gene-expression profile to predict whether it belongs to a clone that has multiplied inside a tumour.
plain_idea.train_on: The gene-expression counts of one T cell at a time, over a fixed set of 11,950 genes (a number I verified in the released gene list). The authors used 2,610,700 cells from 1,445 samples across 14 cancer types, a total I reproduced by summing their Table S1 - but that assembled table is not deposited and would have to be rebuilt from 34 separate public deposits.
plain_idea.predict: A probability that the cell is part of an expanded clone. The true answer comes from sequencing each cell's T-cell receptor, grouping cells that carry an identical receptor sequence into clones, and calling a clone expanded if it is more than 1.5 times the median clone size in that sample. Nothing downloadable contains that answer as a column.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Receptor sequencing roughly doubles the cost of a single-cell experiment, so thousands of published expression-only datasets could be re-read for immune-clone dynamics if expansion were predictable from expression alone. Cancer immunologists and clinical-trial groups choosing checkpoint-inhibitor patients would use it. Even a failure would tell us how much of a clone's proliferation history is written in its current transcriptome.

ml_idea: Two framings, and both die for the same reason. (1) Reproduce or improve on scXpand. This requires the labelled database, which is deposited nowhere - the data availability statement gives only accessions plus 'available from the lead contact upon request', the 1.39 GB Figshare record holds five model checkpoints and a gene list and nothing else, and the authors' own specification (docs/data_format.rst) confirms that 'expansion' is a column the user must build. Building it means rebuilding 34 heterogeneous deposits (one single file is 2.0 GB compressed), one of which, Bassez et al. 2021, sits behind an EGA data access committee and a Data Transfer Agreement. (2) Honestly re-evaluate the released models on a stratified split, which is normally the cheap legitimate project here - except the authors already did it and published the result in the spreadsheets I parsed: 12 external datasets by five models, stratified by tissue and T-cell subtype, a label-permutation negative control, a training-set subsampling curve, a threshold-sensitivity sweep and a patient-level-versus-sample-level relabelling check. That is the checklist's one fatal C2 configuration - open reproducible models plus honest evaluation already done. What is left is a genuine observation worth writing to the authors, which I verified in their own files and code and which they have not framed as a limitation: the clone identifier is built as patient + clonotype + 'imputed_labels', where 'imputed_labels' is a cell subtype derived by MAGIC imputation from CD8A, CD8B, CD4 and FOXP3 expression - the model's own input features - so the ground-truth clone membership depends partly on the features. Their own stratified tables show the consequence: the headline 0.924 becomes 0.762 inside tumour CD8-positive T cells, and CD8A is the third-ranked explanatory gene. A one-page note, with a specific experiment they could run (shuffle only the subtype term and re-derive the labels), is the deliverable here - not a project. One smaller file-level observation: Table S3's 'Missing Genes per Dataset' column shows the Wang melanoma dataset was scored with 1,086 of 11,950 genes (9.1%) silently zero-filled and still returned 0.937, which deserves a sentence somewhere.

effort.compute_note: All estimates, nothing timed on a model - I ran no training and downloaded no count matrix. hours_to_feature_table and working_set_gb describe only the narrowest route (one Zenodo record, Raw_files.zip at 666,868,659 bytes by HTTP header, through the authors' 90-cell documented notebook to about 36,875 labelled cells); the paper's own scale is hundreds of gigabytes across 34 deposits and a 75.9 GB dense matrix, which I computed from the verified 1,588,309 x 11,950 shape. peak_ram_gb is set by MAGIC imputation on the 92,033 x 23,328 matrix the authors' notebook output shows (about 8.6 GB dense before graph diffusion), which is marginal on 16 GB. needs_gpu is true because anything beyond inference needs one - the authors used a 48 GB card - though running their released logistic, support-vector-machine and LightGBM checkpoints (49 KB to 2.9 MB) is genuinely processor-only. embedding_hours is null because no pretrained backbone is part of the viable baseline. cv_run_minutes covers only inference with the shallow released models on a 37,000-cell subset. My own measured timings: the full-text XML was instant, the Figshare small files downloaded in seconds, and Europe PMC's supplementary bundle failed to complete twice at roughly 75 KB per second over 540 and 1,700 seconds.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Search every deposited artefact for a per-cell 'expansion' column. Ten minutes, and it kills the project: the 1,393,056,068-byte Figshare record is five model checkpoints plus a gene list, the GitHub repository has no data directory, and the authors' own docs/data_format.rst lists 'expansion' among the fields the user must supply. Second-cheapest, five more minutes: open lambrechtslab.sites.vib.be and confirm that one training cohort (80 samples, 36,701 cells) requires a UZLeuven-VIB data access committee review and a Data Transfer Agreement. Do both before reading the methods.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A at A1, A2, A6 and partly A8, all checked in the files rather than inferred from the abstract. A1 and A2 together are the kill: the labelled 2.6-million-cell database this paper is built on is deposited nowhere. The data availability statement offers only accessions plus 'available from the lead contact upon request'; the 1.39 GB Figshare record contains five trained model checkpoints and a 91 KB gene list and nothing else (I listed and partly downloaded it); Figshare and Zenodo searches for 'scXpand' return no dataset; and the authors' own specification, docs/data_format.rst, confirms that the prediction target 'expansion' is a column the user has to construct by matching scRNA-seq to receptor sequencing barcode by barcode, defining clonotypes from CDR3 nucleotide identity, and thresholding clone size at 1.5 times the per-sample median. A6: rebuilding it means 34 heterogeneous deposits of which one single file is 2,006,028,402 bytes compressed, a 1,588,309 x 11,950 matrix that is 75.9 GB dense, and the authors' own 256 GB / 48 GB-graphics-card workstation. One training cohort (Bassez et al. 2021, 80 samples, 36,701 cells) additionally needs an EGA data access committee review and a Data Transfer Agreement, which I confirmed on the laboratory's page. A8 fails partially and precisely: the clone identifier is patient + clonotype + an expression-imputed cell subtype, so ground-truth clone membership depends partly on the model's own input features, and the authors' spreadsheets quantify the cost - the headline 0.924 area under the curve falls to 0.762 inside tumour CD8-positive T cells, with CD8A the third-ranked explanatory gene. Everything else about this paper is excellent and that is precisely why it is a bad project: the code is MIT, the models are CC BY 4.0 and processor-runnable, every headline count reconciles exactly against my own sums of Table S1 (1,055,922 tumour, 532,387 blood, 963 samples, 482 test samples, 2,610,700 total), and the honest evaluation a re-analyst would normally contribute has already been published - 12 external datasets by five models, stratification by tissue and subtype, a label-permutation negative control, a subsampling curve and a threshold sweep. That is the one C2 configuration the checklist calls fatal: open, reproducible models with honest evaluation already done. The salvageable output is a one-page note to the authors about the subtype term inside their clone identifier and the 1,086 silently zero-filled genes in one test dataset, not a project.
